blocks.text: 先说对 Anthropic 粉丝来说的好消息。2026 年上半年到 2025 年上半年，公司营收增长了十四倍，达到 163 亿美元。账面上有 800 亿美元亏损，但这主要是一项与底层业务无关的会计处理。把这部分以及员工薪酬等其他费用剔除后，2026 年上半年调整后利润为 16.2 亿美元。我之前问过，AI 能否赚到足够的钱养活自己，Anthropic 的 S-1 给出的答案似乎是：至少对这家公司、至少就目前而言，能。

blocks.text: Anthropic 比 OpenAI 或 Elon Musk 克制得多，而且这似乎正在带来回报。（Anthropic 只把 OpenAI 和 Google 列为竞争对手。Elon，下次好运！）这家公司从未发布过 AI 图像生成器、AI 版 TikTok 克隆或 AI 老婆。它专注于编程和网络安全这类任务，死死盯住计算机最容易做的事：更多的计算机。它还聚焦企业市场，这个市场比消费者市场更稳定。它的净收入留存率是 900%。相当不错！这些收入也不来自消费者。2026 年上半年，约四分之三的客户每年支出至少 10 万美元。

blocks.text: 有一些长期承诺，凸显出 Anthropic 面临的扩张压力有多大。当然，第 64 页上采购承诺和租赁协议一栏留了空，第 137 页上关于 2030 年 12 月 31 日之前预计支出的金额也留了个挺扎眼的空。不过我们知道，这些承诺一直延续到 2045 年。

blocks.text: 好在有一节“承诺与或有事项”能帮上点忙。不可撤销的采购承诺有固定最低总额 2656 亿美元，期限在 1 到 20 年之间。截至 6 月 30 日未经审计的数据，公司还有“主要与算力和基础设施容量相关”的租赁协议尚未开始，金额为 3214 亿美元。此后，Anthropic 又签订了新的算力和基础设施协议，总额约 2450 亿美元，期限同样在 1 到 20 年之间。还有一些尚未最终敲定的交易，Anthropic 估计成本在 1250 亿到 1500 亿美元之间。此外还有金额可变的算力承诺。

blocks.text: 所以要兑现这些承诺，Anthropic 的增长必须继续以惊人的速度推进。Anthropic 没有给出未来承诺的付款时间表，但 PitchBook 分析师 Harrison Rolfes 的模型估算，2027 到 2030 年每年约需 900 亿美元，这意味着要有 1880 亿美元的收入，才能让当前的成本与算力之比保持稳定。“对这家公司来说，增长不是可选项，”他写道，“合同就是建立在增长之上的。”

blocks.text: Claude 已经在人类的指导下构建 Claude。在风险因素中，Anthropic 警告说它已经锁定在这条路线上。这显然要付出代价：用 AI 开发更多 AI“可能导致我们模型能力的进步速度，超过我们开发、验证和实施相应安全、对齐与安保措施的能力”。如果我理解得没错，Anthropic 是在说，它的业务依赖于用自己可能并未完全理解的工作如此快速地构建新模型，以至于出于商业原因，它实际上被迫去做可能对所有人都有风险的事情。这也是为什么风险因素里会出现一堆关于“灾难性”伤害的存在性危险以及“各种形式的感知能力”发展的古怪内容。

blocks.text: The Anthropic S-1 seems to have provided the financial justification for the company to spend as much as it possibly can on compute. If you are the kind of person who wonders if Anthropic is doing its level best to build a machine god while convincing Wall Street it’s in the business of selling IT contracts, Anthropic has just offered a handy solution: Doing a bunch of things that look like you’re trying to build the machine god is the only way to avoid going bankrupt.

blocks.text: Forget about the machine god for a minute. At least in my read of the S-1, it seems like Anthropic is pinning the future of its company to dramatic growth; it has to, in order to meet its fixed costs. You don’t have to be an AI skeptic to lift an eyebrow at these numbers. But if you are skeptical that dramatic recursive self-improvement is possible — in the way the business plan seems to require — this doesn’t look like a good investment.

blocks.text: Let’s start with the good news for Anthropic fans. The company’s revenue grew fourteen times to $16.3 billion between the first half of 2026 and the first half of 2025. There’s an $80 billion loss, but it’s largely an accounting thing that isn’t relevant to the underlying business. If we remove that, and some other charges, including employee compensation, we’re looking at $1.62 billion in adjusted income in the first half of 2026. I’ve asked before if AI can make enough money to pay for itself, and the answer from Anthropic’s S-1 appears to be, at least for this company, at least right now, yes.

blocks.text: What’s more, Anthropic has a disadvantage against a rival like Google. It doesn’t have multiple paths to revenue — and Google does. Google can also wrap its AI into other products businesses already use. Remember when Microsoft Teams ate Slack? It wasn’t because Teams was the better product; Microsoft just had better distribution, since Teams was bundled with other programs companies were already paying for. Having the best model matters more for cybersecurity — one area Anthropic is targeting for growth — than for instant messaging software, but it’s hard to compete on distribution.

blocks.text: Fortunately, there’s a “Commitments and contingencies” section that can help us out a little. There’s a fixed minimum of non-cancelable purchase commitments that total $265.6 billion, with terms between one and 20 years. The company has lease agreements “primarily related to compute and infrastructure capacity” that haven’t yet commenced of $321.4 billion, as of the unaudited June 30th figures. After that, Anthropic entered new compute and infrastructure agreements totaling about $245 billion, again with terms between one and 20 years. There’s some other transactions that haven’t yet been finalized, which Anthropic estimates as costing $125 billion to $150 billion. There are also other compute commitments that are variable.

blocks.text: So to meet those commitments, Anthropic’s growth must continue at breakneck speed. Anthropic doesn’t give us a payment schedule for its future commitments, but analyst Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook models it at about $90 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, which means $188 billion in revenue to keep the current ratio of cost to compute stable. “Growth is not optional for this company,” he writes. “The contracts assume it.”

blocks.text: As enterprise software, it makes sense for Anthropic to target companies’ IT budgets. Conveniently, cybersecurity is a place where you will absolutely get your shit rekt if you are not constantly up to date — everyone there has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic. Of course, AI is part of the problem; hackers can use it to brute-force stuff they couldn’t do before. Plus, the products themselves are also causing headaches thanks to a partner’s sloppy fuck-up of security protocols around AI agents.

blocks.text: Frontier labs need high-margin products to avoid a race to the bottom on token pricing, notes Burke. That made something else stand out to me: Opus 5.5 reduced customer costs by 40 percent over Opus 5. Now, Anthropic says that lower cost means more usage, which lets the company preserve its margins. If you assume that cost reduction happens every time a new model is released, pretty soon you wind up with tasks at a fraction of the price.

blocks.text: But the pressure for growth is pretty undeniable. That’s where recursive self-improvement, with minimal or no supervision, comes in. “More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn, more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more efficiently.” Based on the general rhetoric Anthropic has about the apocalypse or whatever, it expects to hit dramatic recursive self-improvement, maybe soon.

blocks.text: Claude is already building Claude under human direction. In its risk factors, Anthropic warns that it’s locked in to that approach. That comes with a clear tradeoff, since using AI to develop more AI “may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures.” If I am reading that right, Anthropic is saying that its business relies on building new models so fast, using work it may not fully understand, that it is essentially forced, for business reasons, to do stuff that may be risky to everyone. Which is why we’ve got a bunch of weird stuff about the existential hazards of “catastrophic” harm and the development of “forms of sentience” in the risk factors.
